chapters.title: Doing: Making the Best Action Choices

chapterBreakdown.gentle: A trusted system can still leave one practical question: what should you do now? David Allen's point in this chapter is that action choices depend on present conditions. Context, time, energy, and priority all shape what makes sense in the moment. GTD helps by narrowing the real menu instead of pretending one action is always best in every situation.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Doing in GTD means choosing from a current system according to context, time, energy, and priority. Chapter 9 argues that the best next move depends on the moment you are actually in, not only on abstract importance.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: A good list does not choose for you by magic. Allen's answer is filters. Where you are, how much time you have, how much energy you have, and what matters all decide what the best live move is.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A trusted system can still leave several valid actions in front of you. The hard part is not always finding something worth doing. It is choosing what fits the present moment best. Allen uses Chapter 9 to bring GTD into that live decision space. Once the system is current enough to trust, action choice becomes a matter of reading the conditions of the moment instead of guessing blindly.

Context is the first filter because not every action can be done everywhere. A phone call, a laptop task, and an errand may all be real options, but the setting immediately changes which of them belongs on the live menu. The chapter treats that as practical clarity, not as a limitation to resent.

Time matters next because a ten-minute gap and an open afternoon do not support the same action. Some work fits a short window. Some does not. Allen's point is that the best next move changes with the size of the window available. Ignoring that fact makes choice less intelligent, not more principled.

Energy matters for the same reason. A low-energy evening and a sharp morning create different realistic choices. The chapter does not present that as failure of character. It treats present energy as part of the action environment. Choosing well means matching the demand of the task to the energy actually available.

Priority still matters, but it matters inside those real conditions. The most important item in the abstract is not automatically the best next move if the current context, time, and energy cannot support it. GTD does not erase importance. It grounds importance in the moment where action has to happen.

The chapter gives higher horizons a bounded role as wider framing above the ground level, but the daily choice still happens here, inside live conditions. Doing works when the system and the moment meet cleanly. That is what makes the choice practical instead of theatrical.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The GTD system reaches the point of engagement here. Once review has made the lists current, the next question is not what matters in the abstract, but what action fits now. Allen's answer is that doing depends on filters: context, time, energy, and priority. Those filters narrow the live menu so a person can choose from the system intelligently instead of reacting from pressure alone.

Context matters because availability is real. Some actions can be done in the current setting and some cannot. A good next action is not simply one that matters; it is one that is available inside the conditions you actually have. That makes the system more practical, because it meets the person where the work is happening.

Time matters because choice changes with the size of the opening. A small window and a large window do not call for the same move. The chapter pushes against the fantasy that the best action floats above circumstance unchanged. Allen's logic says that circumstances are part of the selection process.

Energy matters because the same list produces different good choices at different levels of mental and physical readiness. The chapter uses energy not as an excuse but as a constraint to acknowledge honestly. Matching the task to the available energy is part of choosing well from a trusted system.

Priority matters inside those filters. It does not disappear, but it does not overrule everything else mechanically either. The best move now is shaped by importance, yet it is also shaped by what the moment can genuinely support. That is what turns GTD from a list system into a situated decision system.

The chapter only gives the higher horizons a bounded supporting role. They frame the wider meaning of commitments, but they do not replace the ground-level act of choosing from present options. Doing remains a live choice from a current system under current conditions.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A current system does not erase the hardest part of work. It sharpens it. Several actions may be valid, and you still have to choose the one that fits this moment best. Allen's move in Chapter 9 is to stop pretending that the best action lives outside conditions. Context, time, energy, and priority decide what makes sense now.

Context is the first cut. If the action cannot be done where you are, it is not the live move no matter how noble it looks on paper. Time is the second cut. Ten minutes and two hours are not the same world. Energy is the third cut. A task that fits a sharp morning may be the wrong call at the end of a drained day.

Priority still matters, but it matters inside those cuts. The abstract top item is not automatically the best next move if the moment cannot carry it. Allen's system is tougher than simple priority worship because it forces importance to face reality.

This is what makes doing practical instead of dramatic. The goal is not to announce allegiance to the theoretically highest task. The goal is to choose the best available action from the system you trust under the conditions you actually have.

The higher horizons stay above this ground game as wider framing, but the choice still happens down here. GTD does not remove the need to choose. It gives the choice a cleaner set of filters so the move is less random and less performative.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A trusted system does not remove the difficulty of choice. It changes the form of it. Once the lists are current, the person is no longer asking what exists to do. The harder question is what fits this moment best. Allen uses Chapter 9 to keep that question grounded in conditions instead of drifting into abstract importance alone.

The chapter's first move is to assume a trustworthy current system. That matters because action choice becomes distorted when the menu itself is doubtful. Once trust is in place, the deciding work shifts to filtering. Context is the first filter because availability is real. Some actions can be taken where you are and some cannot. That is not a weakness in the system. It is part of what makes the choice honest.

Time and energy deepen the same logic. A short window and a long window do not support the same move. A sharp hour and a drained hour do not support the same move. Allen's chapter treats these as decision conditions, not as excuses. The best next action changes because the live constraints change.

Priority still matters, but only inside those constraints. The chapter resists the fantasy that importance alone can dictate the correct action independent of setting, time, and energy. A theoretically higher-priority task may still be the wrong next move if the current moment cannot sustain it. That does not weaken priority. It places priority inside reality.

The chapter also gives higher horizons a bounded supporting role. They help frame why work matters, but they do not replace the ground-level choice process. Doing still happens through present filters. The horizons stay above the move rather than becoming a substitute for it.

The hard edge is that people often keep choosing as if present conditions are irrelevant. They select by abstract importance, then stall because the chosen task does not fit the real window or the real energy available. Allen's system is practical precisely because it lets the moment answer back. It narrows the menu until the best available move is both meaningful and possible.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
GTD becomes a live decision method here. Review made the system current enough to trust, but current lists do not automatically choose the action. Allen's contribution here is to show that action choice depends on filters: context, time, energy, and priority. Those filters translate a trustworthy system into a fitting move under real conditions.

Context matters because a next action is only meaningful if it is available in the environment you actually have. Time matters because windows differ in size and therefore in what they can honestly support. Energy matters because the same task can be a smart move in one state and a poor move in another. The chapter treats all three as practical constraints that make choice more accurate, not less serious.

Priority enters after those conditions are visible. It helps decide among the genuinely available options, but it does not float above the rest untouched. Allen's point is that importance must meet reality at ground level. Otherwise the person keeps choosing noble-looking tasks that the moment cannot carry, then confuses the resulting stall for lack of discipline.

The six horizons remain in the background as a wider framing device, but the chapter keeps doing at the ground level. The question is not what matters in the broadest possible sense. The question is what action fits now given the system, the moment, and the larger meaning already held above it.

This is why GTD action choice is neither random nor rigid. It is structured responsiveness. A good system gives the options. The present conditions shape the best available move among them. That is what makes the method usable in live work instead of only admirable in planning mode.

The chapter's failure mode is choosing as if conditions are irrelevant. When people ignore context, time, or energy, they keep selecting actions from theory and then running into practical mismatch. The filters exist to prevent exactly that waste.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A current GTD system still does not hand you one glowing answer. It hands you a field of real options and forces a sharper question: which move fits now? Allen's answer is not hype, instinct, or blind priority worship. It is filters. Context, time, energy, and priority decide what counts as the best live move.

Context makes the first cut. If the setting cannot support that move, it is off the board no matter how righteous it sounds. Time makes the second cut. A ten-minute window and a free afternoon are different universes. Energy makes the third cut. A drained state cannot honestly carry the same choice as a sharp one.

Priority still matters, but only after the other cuts are real. That is what makes this chapter tougher than generic advice. It refuses to let theoretical importance pretend it can ignore the moment. The top task on paper is not automatically the right next move if the present conditions cannot cash it out.

The higher horizons stay above the ground game as framing, not as a replacement for present-tense choice. You still have to choose down here, in the real room, with the real clock, and the real battery.

This is what keeps GTD from becoming either mood-driven or robotic. The system provides the candidate moves. The filters make the choice honest. Without them, you keep selecting for abstract virtue and paying for practical mismatch.

The warning is blunt: if you choose as if context, time, and energy do not matter, you are choosing from fantasy. The method works because reality gets a vote before importance gets the final word.
